arXiv:1601.05189v1 [math.AP] 20 Jan 2016

A Nonlocal Dispersal SIS Epidemic Model in Heterogeneous Environment

Fei-Ying Yang Affiliation: School of Mathematics and Statistics,    Wan-Tong Li ††thanks: Corresponding author (wtli@lzu.edu.cn). Affiliation: Key Laboratory of Applied Mathematics and Complex Systems,    Liang Zhang Affiliation: Lanzhou University, Lanzhou, Gansu, 730000, P.R. China
Abstract

This article is concerned with a nonlocal dispersal susceptible-infected-susceptible (SIS) epidemic model with Neumann boundary condition, where the rates of disease transmission and recovery are assumed to be spatially heterogeneous and the total population number is constant. We first introduce the basic reproduction number R0R_{0} and then discuss the existence, uniqueness and stability of steady states of the nonlocal dispersal SIS epidemic model in terms of R0R_{0}. In particular, we also consider the impacts of the large diffusion rates of the susceptible and infected population on the persistence and extinction of the disease, and these results imply that the nonlocal movement of the susceptible or infected individuals will enhance the persistence of the disease. Additionally, our analytical results also suggest that the spatial heterogeneity tends to boost the spread of the disease. We have to emphasize that the main difficulty is that a lack of regularizing effect occurs.

Keywords: Nonlocal dispersal, The basic reproduction number, Disease-free equilibrium, Endemic equilibrium.

AMS Subject Classification (2010): 35B40, 45A05, 45F05, 47G20.

1 Introduction

This paper is concerned with the following nonlocal dispersal SIS epidemic model

{∂S∂t=dS​∫ΩJ⁡(x−y)​(S⁡(y,t)−S⁡(x,t))​dy−β⁡(x)​S​IS+I+γ⁡(x)​I,x∈Ω,t>0,∂I∂t=dI​∫ΩJ⁡(x−y)​(I⁡(y,t)−I⁡(x,t))​dy+β⁡(x)​S​IS+I−γ⁡(x)​I,x∈Ω,t>0,S(x,0)=S0(x),I(x,0)=I0(x),x∈Ω,\begin{cases}\frac{\partial S}{\partial t}=d_{S}\int_{\Omega}J(x-y)(S(y,t)-S(x,t))dy-\frac{\beta(x)SI}{S+I}+\gamma(x)I,&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ \frac{\partial I}{\partial t}=d_{I}\int_{\Omega}J(x-y)(I(y,t)-I(x,t))dy+\frac{\beta(x)SI}{S+I}-\gamma(x)I,&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ S(x,0)=S_{0}(x),~I(x,0)=I_{0}(x),&x\in\Omega,\end{cases} (1.1)

where, Ω\Omega is a bounded domain; S⁡(x,t)S(x,t) and I⁡(x,t)I(x,t) denote the density of susceptible and infected individuals at location xx and time tt, respectively; dSd_{S} and dId_{I} are positive diffusion coefficients for the susceptible and infected individuals; β⁡(x)\beta(x) and γ⁡(x)\gamma(x) are positive continuous functions on Ω¯\bar{\Omega} that represent the rates of disease transmission and recovery at xx. It is known from [2] that the term S​IS+I\frac{SI}{S+I} is a Lipschitz continuous function of SS and II in the open first quadrant, we can extend its definition to the entire first quadrant by defining it to be zero when either S=0S=0 or I=0I=0. Throughout the whole paper, we assume that the initial infected individuals are positive without other description, that is

∫ΩI⁡(x,0)​𝑑x>0,with​S0​(x)≥0​and​I0​(x)≥0​for​x∈Ω\int_{\Omega}I(x,0)dx>0,~\text{with}~S_{0}(x)\geq 0~\text{and}~I_{0}(x)\geq 0~\text{for}~x\in\Omega

and the dispersal kernel function JJ satisfies

(J) J⁡(x)∈C⁡(Ω¯),J⁡(0)>0,J⁡(x)=J⁡(−x)≥0,∫ℝNJ⁡(x)​𝑑x=1J(x)\in C(\bar{\Omega}),J(0)>0,~J(x)=J(-x)\geq 0,~\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}J(x)dx=1 and ∫ΩJ⁡(x−y)​𝑑y≢1\int_{\Omega}J(x-y)dy\not\equiv 1 for any x∈Ωx\in\Omega.

By the standard theory of semigroups of linear bounded operator [29], we know from [25] that (1.1) admits a unique positive solution (S∗​(x,t),I∗​(x,t))(S_{*}(x,t),I_{*}(x,t)), which is continuous with respect to xx and tt. Let

N:=∫Ω(S0​(x)+I0​(x))​𝑑x.N:=\int_{\Omega}(S_{0}(x)+I_{0}(x))dx.

If we add the first equation and the second equation of (1.1) and integrate it on Ω\Omega, then there is

∂∂t​∫Ω(S⁡(x,t)+I⁡(x,t))​𝑑x=0​for all​t>0.\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_{\Omega}(S(x,t)+I(x,t))dx=0~~\text{for all}~t>0.

This implies that the total population size is constant, that is

∫Ω(S⁡(x,t)+I⁡(x,t))​𝑑x=N​for all​t≥0.\int_{\Omega}(S(x,t)+I(x,t))dx=N~~\text{for all}~t\geq 0.

Note that (1.1) is the nonlocal counterpart of the following SIS epidemic reaction-diffusion model

{∂S∂t=dS​Δ​S−β⁡(x)​S​IS+I+γ⁡(x)​I,x∈Ω,t>0,∂I∂t=dI​Δ​I+β⁡(x)​S​IS+I−γ⁡(x)​I,x∈Ω,t>0,∂νS=∂νI=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,\begin{cases}\frac{\partial S}{\partial t}=d_{S}\Delta S-\frac{\beta(x)SI}{S+I}+\gamma(x)I,~&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \frac{\partial I}{\partial t}=d_{I}\Delta I+\frac{\beta(x)SI}{S+I}-\gamma(x)I,~&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \partial_{\nu}S=\partial_{\nu}I=0,~&x\in\partial\Omega,t>0,\end{cases} (1.2)

in which ν\nu is the outward unit normal vector on ∂Ω\partial\Omega. As is well known, (1.2) is first proposed and considered by Allen et al. [2], where they mainly discussed the impact of spatial heterogeneity of environment and movement of individuals on the persistence and extinction of a disease. After that, their results were extended by Peng and Liu [30], in which they proved that the endemic equilibrium was globally asymptotically stable if it exists and this result confirms the conjecture proposed in [2]. Meanwhile, Peng [31] provided further understanding regarding the roles of large or small migration rates of the susceptible and infected population on the spatial persistence and extinction of the epidemic disease, and these results were further extended in [33]. Moreover, Peng and Zhao in [32] considered (1.2) when the rates of disease transmission and recovery are assumed to be spatially heterogeneous and temporally periodic. For other results about SIS epidemic models with spatial heterogeneity, one can also see [1, 3, 23].

The nonlocal dispersal as a long range process can be better to describe some natural phenomena in many situations [4, 18]. Thus, nonlocal dispersal equations have attracted much attention and have been used to model different dispersal phenomena in population ecology, material science and neurology, see [5, 22, 25, 34, 43, 9, 39]. For the study of the nonlocal problem, we refer to [14, 15, 38, 50] about the asymptotic behavior, [35, 7, 41, 12, 28, 26, 27] about the traveling waves and entire solutions when Ω=ℝ\Omega=\mathbb{R} and [10, 8, 40, 13, 47, 46] about the stationary solutions. In particular, the spectrum properties of nonlocal dispersal operators and their essential difference comparing with the random operators are contained in [11, 12, 19, 39, 35, 37]. Nowadays, the diffusion process is described by an integral operators such as J∗u−u=∫ℝNJ⁡(x−y)​u​(y)​𝑑y−uJ*u-u=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}J(x-y)u(y)dy-u in epidemiology, see [49, 48] and the references therein.

The present paper is devoted to the dynamic behavior of system (1.1). It is well-known that the basic reproduction number denoted by R0R_{0} is an important threshold parameter to discuss the dynamic behavior of the epidemic models. For system (1.1), it is natural to ask what the basic reproduction number is and how it decides the dynamic behavior of (1.1). As one of the important quantities in epidemiology, the basic reproduction number R0R_{0} of an infectious disease is defined to be the expected number of secondary cases produced, in a completely susceptible population, by a typical infective individual (see, e.g., [24] and the reference therein). For autonomous epidemic models, Diekmann et al.[16] introduced R0R_{0} by using the next generation operators. Driessche and Watmough [17] established the theory of R0R_{0} for compartment ODE models. Thieme [42] further developed a general theory of spectral bound and reproduction number for the infinite-dimensional population structure and time heterogeneity. For a nonlocal and time-delayed reaction-diffusion model of dengue fever, Wang and Zhao [44] gave the definition of R0R_{0} via a next generation operator and proved the threshold dynamics in terms of R0R_{0}. Recently, Wang and Zhao [45] presented the theory of R0R_{0} for reaction-diffusion epidemic models with compartment structure and in particular, characterized R0R_{0} by means of the principal eigenvalue of an elliptic eigenvalue problem. In the current study, motivated by the works in [42, 44, 45], we intend to introduce the basic reproduction number R0R_{0} for model (1.1), and give its characterization. We further prove that R0−1R_{0}-1 has the same sign as

μp​(dI)=supφ∈L2​(Ω)φ≠0−dI2∫Ω∫ΩJ(x−y)(φ(y)−φ(x))2dydx+∫Ω(β(x)−γ(x))φ2(x)dx∫Ωφ2​(x)​𝑑x,\displaystyle\mu_{p}(d_{I})=\sup_{\scriptstyle\varphi\in L^{2}(\Omega)\atop\scriptstyle\varphi\neq 0}\frac{-\frac{d_{I}}{2}\int_{\Omega}\int_{\Omega}J(x-y)(\varphi(y)-\varphi(x))^{2}dydx+\int_{\Omega}(\beta(x)-\gamma(x))\varphi^{2}(x)dx}{\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{2}(x)dx},

which is of interest by itself. In general, μp​(dI)\mu_{p}(d_{I}) may not be the principal eigenvalue of the nonlocal operator

ℳ⁡[u]​(x):=dI​∫ΩJ⁡(x−y)​(u⁡(y)−u⁡(x))​𝑑y+(β⁡(x)−γ⁡(x))​u​(x),\mathcal{M}[u](x):=d_{I}\int_{\Omega}J(x-y)(u(y)-u(x))dy+(\beta(x)-\gamma(x))u(x),

which may lead some essential difference between the nonlocal dispersal problem and the reaction-diffusion problem, see [22, 11, 35, 39, 40]. Thus, we may not characterize the basic reproduction number of system (1.1) through the eigenvalue problem corresponding to the nonlocal operators. To overcome this difficulty, we use the basic theory developed in [42] to give the definition of the basic reproduction number of system (1.1).

After then, we are most concerned with the global stability of the disease-free equilibrium and the endemic equilibrium of system (1.1). It is obtained that the disease-free equilibrium is unique and globally stable when R0<1R_{0}<1, which implies that the disease will be extinct in this case. By the sub-super solution method, we give the existence of the endemic equilibrium, and motivated by the method in [6], obtain its uniqueness as R0>1R_{0}>1. Generally, the stability of the endemic equilibrium is very difficult to be proved. When dS=dId_{S}=d_{I}, however, the global stability of the endemic equilibrium can be shown by constructing some auxiliary problems in this paper. On the basis of Lyapunov stability theorem, the global stability of the endemic equilibrium can be also obtained if the rate of disease transmission is proportional to the rate of the disease recovery. These results imply that the disease will be persistent when R0>1R_{0}>1. Finally, we discuss the effect of the diffusion rates dSd_{S} and dId_{I} on the disease transmission. Necessarily, we find that the nonlocal movement of the susceptible or infected individuals tends to enhance the persistence of the disease. However, there are some difficulties for us to overcome when we prove the above results due to the lack of the regularity of solutions of (1.1) or the stationary solutions corresponding to system (1.1).

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we give the characterization of the reproduction number of system (1.1). The existence, uniqueness and global stability of the disease-free equilibrium are obtained in Section 3. Section 4 is devoted to the existence, uniqueness and global stability of the endemic equilibrium. In Section 5, we discuss the effect of the diffusion rates associated with the susceptible and infected individuals on the disease transmission. Finally, we give a brief discussion to complete the paper.

2 The basic reproduction number

In this section, we will give the definition of the basic reproduction number for system (1.1) and provide its analytical properties. Let X=C⁡(Ω¯)X=C(\bar{\Omega}) be the Banach space of real continuous functions on Ω¯\bar{\Omega}. Throughout this section, XX is considered as an ordered Banach space with a positive cone X+={u∈X|u≥0}X_{+}=\{u\in X|~u\geq 0\}. It is well-known that X+X_{+} is generating, normal and has nonempty interior. Additionally, an operator T:X→XT:X\to X is called positive if T​X+⊆X+TX_{+}\subseteq X_{+}.

Definition 2.1

A closed operator 𝒜\mathscr{A} in XX is called resolvent-positive, if the resolvent set of 𝒜\mathscr{A}, ρ⁡(𝒜)\rho(\mathscr{A}), contains a ray (ω,∞)(\omega,\infty) and (λ​I−𝒜)−1(\lambda I-\mathscr{A})^{-1} is a positive operator for all λ>ω\lambda>\omega.

Definition 2.2

The spectral bound of 𝒜\mathscr{A} is defined by

S⁡(𝒜)=sup{R​e​λ|λ∈σ⁡(𝒜)},S(\mathscr{A})=\sup\{Re\lambda|~\lambda\in\sigma(\mathscr{A})\},

where σ⁡(𝒜)\sigma(\mathscr{A}) denotes the spectrum of 𝒜\mathscr{A}. The spectral radius of 𝒜\mathscr{A} is defined as

r⁡(𝒜)=sup{|λ|;λ∈σ⁡(𝒜)}.r(\mathscr{A})=\sup\{|\lambda|;~\lambda\in\sigma(\mathscr{A})\}.
Theorem 2.3 ([42])

Let 𝒜\mathscr{A} be the generator of a C0−C_{0}-semigroup SS on the ordered Banach space XX with a normal and generating cone X+X_{+}. Then, 𝒜\mathscr{A} is a resolvent-positive if and only if SS is a positive semigroup, i.e., S⁡(t)​X+⊂X+S(t)X_{+}\subset X_{+} for all t≥0t\geq 0. If 𝒜\mathscr{A} is resolvent-positive, then

(λ​I−𝒜)−1​x=limb→∞∫0beλ​t​S​(t)​x​𝑑t,λ>S⁡(𝒜),x∈X.(\lambda I-\mathscr{A})^{-1}x=\lim_{b\to\infty}\int_{0}^{b}e^{\lambda t}S(t)xdt,~\lambda>S(\mathscr{A}),~x\in X.
Theorem 2.4 ([42])

Let ℬ\mathscr{B} be a resolvent-positive operator on XX, S⁡(ℬ)<0S(\mathscr{B})<0 and 𝒜=𝒞+ℬ\mathscr{A}=\mathscr{C}+\mathscr{B} a positive perturbation of ℬ\mathscr{B}. If 𝒜\mathscr{A} is resolvent-positive, S⁡(𝒜)S(\mathscr{A}) has the same sign as r⁡(−𝒞​ℬ−1)−1r(-\mathscr{C}\mathscr{B}^{-1})-1.

For applying the basic theory in [42] to discuss the basic reproduction number of system (1.1), we first consider the eigenvalue problem

ℳ⁡[u]​(x):=dI​∫ΩJ⁡(x−y)​(u⁡(y)−u⁡(x))​𝑑y+β⁡(x)​u​(x)−γ⁡(x)​u​(x)=−λ​u​(x)​in​Ω,\mathcal{M}[u](x):=d_{I}\int_{\Omega}J(x-y)(u(y)-u(x))dy+\beta(x)u(x)-\gamma(x)u(x)=-\lambda u(x)~~\text{in}~\Omega, (2.1)

which will be also used to obtain the main result in this section. Define

λp​(dI)=infφ∈L2​(Ω)φ≠0dI2​∫Ω∫ΩJ⁡(x−y)​(φ⁡(y)−φ⁡(x))2​𝑑y​𝑑x+∫Ω(γ⁡(x)−β⁡(x))​φ2​(x)​𝑑x∫Ωφ2​(x)​𝑑x.\lambda_{p}(d_{I})=\inf_{\scriptstyle\varphi\in L^{2}(\Omega)\atop\scriptstyle\varphi\neq 0}\frac{\frac{d_{I}}{2}\int_{\Omega}\int_{\Omega}J(x-y)(\varphi(y)-\varphi(x))^{2}dydx+\int_{\Omega}(\gamma(x)-\beta(x))\varphi^{2}(x)dx}{\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{2}(x)dx}.

It is well-known that λp​(dI)\lambda_{p}(d_{I}) can be the unique principal eigenvalue of (2.1), see [11, 22, 39, 35].

Lemma 2.5

Set m(x)=−dI∫ΩJ(x−y)dy+β(x)−γ(x)m(x)=-d_{I}\int_{\Omega}J(x-y)dy+\beta(x)-\gamma(x). Suppose there is some x0∈I​n​t​(Ω)x_{0}\in Int(\Omega) satisfying that m⁡(x0)=maxΩ¯⁡m⁡(x)m(x_{0})=\max_{\bar{\Omega}}m(x), and the partial derivatives of m⁡(x)m(x) up to order N−1N-1 at x0x_{0} are zero. Then, λp​(dI)\lambda_{p}(d_{I}) is the unique principal eigenvalue of (2.1) and its corresponding eigenfunction φ\varphi is positive and continuous on Ω¯\bar{\Omega}.

Lemma 2.6

λp​(dI)\lambda_{p}(d_{I}) is the principal eigenvalue of (2.1) if and only if

λp​(dI)<minΩ¯⁡{dI​∫ΩJ⁡(x−y)​𝑑y+γ⁡(x)−β⁡(x)}.\lambda_{p}(d_{I})<\min_{\bar{\Omega}}\left\{d_{I}\int_{\Omega}J(x-y)dy+\gamma(x)-\beta(x)\right\}.

The proof of Lemma 2.6 is the same as Proposition 3.2 in [12].

Remark 2.7

Note that λp​(dI)\lambda_{p}(d_{I}) is continuous on JJ, β⁡(x)\beta(x) and γ⁡(x)\gamma(x), see the proof in [11].

Define an operator as follows

Now, consider the nonlocal dispersal problem

∂uI​(x,t)∂t=dI​∫ΩJ⁡(x−y)​(uI​(y,t)−uI​(x,t))​𝑑y−γ⁡(x)​uI​(x,t),\frac{\partial u_{I}(x,t)}{\partial t}=d_{I}\int_{\Omega}J(x-y)(u_{I}(y,t)-u_{I}(x,t))dy-\gamma(x)u_{I}(x,t), (2.7)

where x∈Ωx\in\Omega and t>0t>0. If uI​(x,t)u_{I}(x,t) is thought of as a density of the infected individuals at a point xx at time tt, J⁡(x−y)J(x-y) is thought of as the probability distribution of jumping from location yy to location xx, then ∫ΩJ⁡(y−x)​u​(y,t)​𝑑y\int_{\Omega}J(y-x)u(y,t)dy is the rate at which the infected individuals are arriving at position xx from all other places, and −∫ΩJ(y−x)u(x,t)dy-\int_{\Omega}J(y-x)u(x,t)dy is the rate at which they are leaving location xx to travel to all other sites. By the theory of semigroups of linear operators, we know that the operator AA can generate a uniformly continuous semigroup, denoted by T⁡(t)T(t). Suppose that ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) is the distribution of initial infection at location xx. Then the distribution of those infective members is at time t (as time evolution) is (T​(t)​ϕ)​(x)\left(T(t)\phi\right)(x). ∫0∞ℱ⁡[T⁡(t)​ϕ]​(x)​𝑑t.\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathscr{F}[T(t)\phi](x)dt.

L⁡[ϕ]​(x):=∫0∞ℱ⁡[T⁡(t)​ϕ]​(x)​𝑑t=β⁡(x)​∫0∞T⁡(t)​ϕ​𝑑t.L[\phi](x):=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathscr{F}[T(t)\phi](x)dt=\beta(x)\int_{0}^{\infty}T(t)\phi dt.

(λ​I−A)−1​ϕ=∫0∞e−λ​t​T​(t)​ϕ​𝑑t​for any​λ>S⁡(A),ϕ∈X.(\lambda I-A)^{-1}\phi=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda t}T(t)\phi dt~~\text{for any}~\lambda>S(A),~\phi\in X. (2.8)

Lemma 2.14

−dI∫ΩJ(x−y)(ϕ(y)−ϕ(x))dy+γ(x)ϕ(x)=μβ(x)ϕ(x),x∈Ω.-d_{I}\int_{\Omega}J(x-y)(\phi(y)-\phi(x))dy+\gamma(x)\phi(x)=\mu\beta(x)\phi(x),~~x\in\Omega. (2.10)

and define

Corollary 2.15

If (μ∗,ϕ∗​(x))(\mu^{*},\phi^{*}(x)) with ϕ∗​(x)>0\phi^{*}(x)>0 satisfies the following linear problem

In this section, we major in discussing the existence and stability of the disease-free equilibrium of (1.1). That is, we consider the stationary problem of system (1.1):

{dS​∫ΩJ⁡(x−y)​(S⁡(y)−S⁡(x))​dy=β⁡(x)​S​IS+I−γ⁡(x)​I,x∈Ω,dI​∫ΩJ⁡(x−y)​(I⁡(y)−I⁡(x))​dy=−β⁡(x)​S​IS+I+γ⁡(x)​I,x∈Ω.\begin{cases}d_{S}\int_{\Omega}J(x-y)(S(y)-S(x))dy=\frac{\beta(x)SI}{S+I}-\gamma(x)I,~&x\in\Omega,\\ d_{I}\int_{\Omega}J(x-y)(I(y)-I(x))dy=-\frac{\beta(x)SI}{S+I}+\gamma(x)I,~&x\in\Omega.\end{cases} (3.1)

limt→+∞(S∗​(x,t),I∗​(x,t))=(S~​(x),I~​(x))\lim_{t\to+\infty}(S_{*}(x,t),I_{*}(x,t))=(\tilde{S}(x),\tilde{I}(x))

Remark 3.4

Theorem 3.3 implies that when R0<1R_{0}<1, the epidemic disease will be extinct.

Remark 4.7

Note that when dS=dId_{S}=d_{I}, the epidemic disease will persist as R0>1R_{0}>1. Moreover, if the rate of the disease transmission is proportional to the rate of the disease recovery (i.e β⁡(x)=r​γ​(x)\beta(x)=r\gamma(x) for some positive constant rr), then the epidemic disease will be completely extinct finally as R0≤1R_{0}\leq 1 (i.e r≤1r\leq 1), and will be persistence as R0>1R_{0}>1 (i.e r>1r>1). Particularly, the epidemic disease will be always extinct as R0<1R_{0}<1. The case when dS≠dId_{S}\neq d_{I} and R0>1R_{0}>1 is very complicate. This is a challenging work and we will leave it for further study.

5 The effect of the large diffusion rates

In this section, we discuss the effect of the large diffusion rate on the transmission of the disease. Throughout this section, we always assume that ∫Ωβ⁡(x)​𝑑x>∫Ωγ⁡(x)​𝑑x\int_{\Omega}\beta(x)dx>\int_{\Omega}\gamma(x)dx. Following Corollary 2.13, we know R0>1R_{0}>1 for all dI>0d_{I}>0 in this condition. Then, the positive solution (S~,I~)(\tilde{S},\tilde{I}) of (3.1) exists.

6 Discussion

In the current paper, we firstly give the basic reproduction number R0R_{0} of system (1.1), which is an important threshold value to discuss the dynamic behavior of (1.1). We prove that the disease persists when R0>1R_{0}>1, but when R0<1R_{0}<1, the disease dies out. Moreover, we also consider the effect of the large diffusion rates for the susceptible individuals or the infected individuals on the disease transmission and find that the nonlocal movement of the susceptible individuals or infected individuals will enhance the persistence of the disease.

In Section 2, we have proved the main result Theorem 2.10, and established the relations between R0R_{0} and λp​(dI)\lambda_{p}(d_{I}) even if λp​(dI)\lambda_{p}(d_{I}) is not always a principal eigenvalue of the operator ℳ\mathcal{M} defined by (2.1). Note that if β⁡(x)=β\beta(x)=\beta and γ⁡(x)=γ\gamma(x)=\gamma are all positive constants, then the linear problem

−dI∫ΩJ(x−y)(u(y)−u(x))dy+γu(x)=μβu(x)inΩ-d_{I}\int_{\Omega}J(x-y)(u(y)-u(x))dy+\gamma u(x)=\mu\beta u(x)~~\text{in}~\Omega

admits a principal eigenpair (μp,φ⁡(x))(\mu_{p},\varphi(x)), where μp=γβ\mu_{p}=\frac{\gamma}{\beta}. Thus, it follows from Lemma 2.16 that R0=1μp=βγR_{0}=\frac{1}{\mu_{p}}=\frac{\beta}{\gamma} in this case. By the same discussion as Sections 3 and 4, we have that the disease persists if β>γ\beta>\gamma and the disease dies out if β<γ\beta<\gamma. But when the spatial heterogeneity is concerned, we know from Corollaries 2.12 and 2.13 that the disease may persist even though there are some sites such that β⁡(x)<γ⁡(x)\beta(x)<\gamma(x). That is, the spatial heterogeneity can enhance the spread of the disease. In fact, from [2], xx is a low-risk site if the local disease transmission rate β⁡(x)\beta(x) is lower than the local disease recovery rate γ⁡(x)\gamma(x), and the high-risk site is defined in a similar way. Meanwhile, Ω\Omega is a low-risk domain if ∫Ωβ⁡(x)​𝑑x≤∫Ωγ⁡(x)​𝑑x\int_{\Omega}\beta(x)dx\leq\int_{\Omega}\gamma(x)dx and a high-risk domain if ∫Ωβ⁡(x)​𝑑x>∫Ωγ⁡(x)​𝑑x\int_{\Omega}\beta(x)dx>\int_{\Omega}\gamma(x)dx. In the view of the biological point, Corollary 2.12 implies that the disease may spread even if the habitat of the species is low-risk as long as there is some high-risk site and the movement of the infected individuals is slow. But the quick movement of the infected individuals may suppress the spread of the disease. Following Corollary 2.13, we know that the disease will always persist if the species live in a high-risk domain and be extinct if the habitat of the species is filled with the low-risk sites. We hope these results will be useful for the disease control.

Additionally, due to the lack of regularity of stationary solutions of system (1.1), we only discuss the effect of the large diffusion rates of the susceptible individuals or the infected individuals on the disease transmission. For other cases, there will be left for the future work. Also, we know that the diffusive ability of the species is different, here the diffusive ability represents the diffusive rates and the dispersal distance. Thus, it is more realistic to discuss that the susceptible individuals and the infected individuals have different dispersal strategy, that is the dispersal kernel functions are distinct from each other. This problem is of interest and it may have more complex dynamic results.
